prize_parts.citation: for developing empirical methods to estimate demand, competition and industry dynamics in differentiated-product markets

statement.case_for: B001 remains my first choice after reading the openings. Random-coefficients demand estimation with endogenous prices (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes 1995) and the dynamic-industry framework built around Pakes turned industrial organisation into a quantitative field. The same toolkit is used in merger review, antitrust and regulation, and it has spread into trade, health, environmental and public economics. The core papers date from the 1990s and have had about three decades of use and stress-testing, so the maturity question is settled. The credit also divides more cleanly than in most other shortlisted entries. BLP is a compact three-person core, and Pakes also carries the dynamic-games and production-function strands. Eight of the other ten members, including those who ranked it lower, propose essentially this set or a one-name variant, which suggests the attribution is not seriously contested. I do not treat that as scientific merit, though. My case rests on originality, breadth of use and durability, and I would apply the same standard to B002, B049 and B013.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is whether this is a prize for a toolkit rather than for an economic discovery. Structural IO has known sensitivities to functional form, numerical implementation and weak identification. Seven credited names covering demand estimation, dynamic games, production functions and the 'new empirical IO' make the unit of the prize unclear, and any three-person cut leaves out serious contributors, above all Bresnahan. If the Committee wants a prize with a more substantive finding, B002 (collateral constraints and credit cycles) or B049 (nominal rigidities and monetary policy) would answer that concern better. Their attribution problems are worse, however.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first but names Bresnahan instead of Levinsohn as the third laureate, arguing that Bresnahan's new empirical IO and early differentiated-product demand work is as central as Levinsohn's BLP role. He also keeps B002 to Kiyotaki and Moore to avoid overlap with the 2022 prize.
responses.response: The Bresnahan-versus-Levinsohn question is the real fault line, and I take it seriously. I still prefer Levinsohn. The prize citation is about a method, and the method is a single named paper whose three authors are the identifiable originators. Bresnahan's contribution is an agenda and an early demand-estimation precedent, which is important but a different kind of credit. Naming him over Levinsohn would split BLP and leave a co-author of the central result unrecognised. I agree with Krusell on B002. Kiyotaki and Moore are the clean pair, which is why I would keep it to two names if it came forward as an alternative. That is also what my own opening proposed.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B002 first because collateral constraints and the financial accelerator are conceptually deep and were validated by the post-2008 crisis. He ranks B001 second and puts Bresnahan in the third slot.
responses.response: I agree that Kiyotaki-Moore is an original and well-confirmed mechanism, and I keep B002 as my first alternative. My reservation is the one he raises himself. Gertler's accelerator work is tied to Bernanke, whose 2022 prize makes the credit awkward, and a pair of Kiyotaki and Moore plus the thematic closeness to 2022 leaves less distinctive ground than B001 has. I would not add Gertler just to make a trio. On the third slot I give the same answer as to Krusell. I would sooner honour Levinsohn as a co-author of the central paper than pick a figure whose contribution is the agenda around it.

responses.point: Stromberg ranks B001 first on originality, breadth and durability. He asks whether structural IO is craft rather than discovery and notes that the pooled candidate spans several strands, so the unit of the prize is not obvious.
responses.response: That is the right question to put to my own first choice. The answer is to define the unit narrowly in the citation, as demand and competition estimation in differentiated-product markets, plus the dynamic-industry framework. The argument that this is craft is weakened by what the method delivers. It allows welfare, market power and merger effects to be measured with counterfactuals that earlier reduced-form work could not give. I would not widen the citation to cover production-function estimation or entry-and-reiss-style models, because that would blur the unit of the prize and reopen the attribution problem. I accept that a Committee that wants only discovery-type prizes might reasonably reach a different view.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B050 first. He argues that Melitz and Helpman's heterogeneous-firm framework changed trade theory and that the area is ripe, since Krugman's 2008 prize covered earlier trade theory.
responses.response: I agree that B050 is a strong, well-confirmed candidacy with a clear originator in Melitz (2003), and I ranked it fifth. Two things keep it below B001 for me. First, parallel empirical and theoretical contributions from Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not in the credited names, so the attribution sits partly outside the ballot. Second, trade is the field closest to the 2008 award. Because Boppart and I have co-authored, I weigh his view with care but do not defer to it. His case does not change my preferred configuration.

uncertainties: Whether Levinsohn or Bresnahan should take the third place alongside Pakes and Berry, and whether the Committee would treat the new empirical IO programme as a separate achievement.
Whether the Committee reads this as a methodological toolkit prize or an economic discovery, and how that bears on the common criteria across fields.
How robust the applied BLP-style results are to numerical implementation and identification choices. I rely on background knowledge and have not independently verified citation or adoption counts.
Whether B002 would be read as too close to the 2022 prize, and whether Gertler would be added, since the other macro-finance members propose different names.
statement.conflict_note: Disclosed from my profile, not adjudicated: I have co-authored with Per Krusell (the secretary), Timo Boppart and Richard Friberg, and I am an IIES colleague of Krusell and Boppart. None of these ties involves the B001 candidates, but Krusell and Boppart argue for different configurations. The 2018 Scientific Background cites my own climate work with Golosov, Krusell and Tsyvinski, and none of the shortlisted candidates is connected to it. No connection to Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn or the other B001 names is apparent from the supplied profile.
